docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Python JSON Logger enables you produce JSON logs when using Python's logging package.

JSON logs are machine readable allowing for much easier parsing and ingestion into log aggregation tools.

This library assumes that you are famliar with the logging standard library package; if you are not you should start by reading the official Logging HOWTO.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Standard Library Compatible: Implement JSON logging without modifying your existing log setup.
  • Supports Multiple JSON Encoders: In addition to the standard libary's json module, also supports the orjson, msgspec JSON encoders.
  • Fully Customizable Output Fields: Control required, excluded, and static fields including automatically picking up custom attributes on LogRecord objects. Fields can be renamed before they are output.
  • Encode Any Type: Encoders are customized to ensure that something sane is logged for any input including those that aren't supported by default. For example formatting UUID objects into their string representation and bytes objects into a base 64 encoded string.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Jump right in with our Quickstart Guide to get python-json-logger integrated into your project quickly.

Here's a small taste of what it looks like:

Example Usage
import logging
from pythonjsonlogger.json import JsonFormatter

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())

logger.addHandler(handler)

logger.info("Logging using python-json-logger!", extra={"more_data": True})
# {"message": "Logging using python-json-logger!", "more_data": true}

docs.title: Benchmarking
docs.text: Compare the default JsonFormatter, OrjsonFormatter, and MsgspecFormatter with the opt-in benchmark suite. Measurements cover serialization and complete record formatting. They help you choose a backend for a workload; they do not predict application throughput or handler I/O performance.

docs.title: Complete-formatting summary
docs.text:
These graphs summarize complete record formatting from the baseline results. Bars show the arithmetic mean of the per-version median operation times. Whiskers show the minimum–maximum of those version medians, not individual timing samples.

Speedups average each version's ratio against CPython stdlib JSON for the same workload and Python major/minor version. Only versions with a matching reference contribute. Lower times and higher speedups indicate faster formatting. Each panel starts at zero and has its own scale.

docs.title: Run benchmarks
docs.text:
From a repository checkout, install the benchmark dependencies:

uv sync --python 3.15 --no-default-groups --group benchmark

On CPython, this group installs all three backends. On PyPy, it installs only the stdlib backend and benchmark tools. Cases for unavailable optional encoders are reported as skipped. The published comparison covers standard GIL-enabled CPython 3.10–3.15 and PyPy 3.10–3.12. Each published CPython result must contain all three backends; PyPy results contain stdlib JSON only.

Check every case without collecting performance measurements:

uv run --no-sync pytest benchmarks --benchmark-disable

Collect measurements with warmup and export the results:

mkdir -p benchmark-results
uv run --no-sync pytest benchmarks --benchmark-warmup=on \
  --benchmark-json=benchmark-results/python-3.15.json

You can also use tox with its uv runner:

uvx --with tox-uv tox -e py315-benchmark
uvx --with tox-uv tox -e pypy312-benchmark

Append -benchmark to a supported tox runtime name to benchmark that interpreter. The workflow selects tox's benchmark label with tox -m benchmark. Ordinary test and benchmark environments share version lists in tox.ini, so supported versions are maintained in one place. Use uvx --with tox-uv tox -e benchmark to use the default interpreter. Results go to the environment's envtmpdir, such as .tox/py315-benchmark/tmp/benchmark.json. Pass pytest options after -- to select cases or change measurement settings. For example, use -k unicode to select Unicode workloads. Normal test runs collect only tests/ and do not need the benchmark dependencies.

The manual Benchmark JSON formatters GitHub Actions workflow runs Linux x86-64 benchmarks for the supported CPython and PyPy versions. One tox invocation runs the runtimes sequentially in one job on the same runner. The job uploads a single artifact containing one JSON file per runtime, and its summary contains the comparison tables. Timing differences never fail CI.

docs.title: Measurement methodology
docs.text:
The suite uses pytest-benchmark for pytest integration, automatic calibration, statistics, and JSON export. Run on an otherwise idle machine, use warmup, and repeat runs before interpreting small differences. Benchmarks and Python environments run sequentially; do not run multiple benchmark sessions concurrently on the same machine.

Each backend uses its default formatter configuration. The two measurement layers are:

  • Serialization: jsonify_log_record() on a prepared dictionary, including bytes-to-string conversion in the orjson and msgspec formatters.
  • Formatting: format(LogRecord) on a prepared record, including field extraction, message handling, exception formatting where applicable, and serialization.

Formatter and record construction, payload preparation, correctness checks, and handler I/O are outside the timed operation. Formatters and records are reused. Checks before and after measurement verify expected parsed content and consistent repeated output. Exception records retain exc_info, so formatting includes rendering the traceback on each call; serialization uses prepared exception text.

Workload Payload simple A short string message structured A string message with scalar LogRecord extras nested A dictionary message containing 100 objects with lists and nested metrics unicode A repeated message containing accented text, Japanese text, and emoji rich A dictionary message containing a UTC datetime, UUID, dataclass, bytes, an Enum class, and its members exception A message and a prepared ValueError traceback

Default outputs can differ. Stdlib JSON escapes non-ASCII characters and uses spaces between elements; the other backends emit compact UTF-8. UTC datetime strings use +00:00 for stdlib and orjson, and Z for msgspec. These are comparisons of the supported formatter defaults, including native rich-type support and fallback encoding costs. They are not byte-identical raw encoder comparisons. Bytes are encoded as base64 strings; the Enum class is encoded as a list of member values, and each Enum member is encoded as its value. JSON results record each case's output size.

docs.title: Repetitions, variation, and precision
docs.text:
Warmup and calibration run before timing. pytest-benchmark chooses a batch of iterations per round and repeats those rounds. Statistics describe the per-operation average duration of each round, rather than individual logging call latencies. See the pytest-benchmark glossary.

The generated summary and timing tables record the actual round counts and iterations per round. Calibration and warmup calls are additional and are excluded from those counts. Each runtime has one full suite run; thousands of timing rounds are not thousands of independent suite runs or machines.

Timing tables show median, arithmetic mean, standard deviation (SD), and interquartile range (IQR), all in microseconds per operation. IQR is Q3 minus Q1: the width containing the middle 50% of round averages. Median and IQR are less sensitive to slow outliers than mean and SD. The JSON also retains minimum, maximum, quartiles, and outlier counts.

There is no universally trustworthy number of decimal places in microseconds. The generated summary reports the observed SD relative to the mean, including outliers. Reported times use at most three significant digits; spreads and speedups use at most two. This is display rounding, not a claim of accuracy. Batching reduces timer overhead, but cannot eliminate scheduler, garbage collection, CPU frequency, or hosted-runner variation. Do not interpret the final displayed digit as a reliable performance difference. Check IQR and SD, and repeat complete runs on the same machine before drawing conclusions about small differences.

Timing plots use labeled horizontal bars, with one panel per workload and measurement layer. Speedup plots use two panels (serialization and complete formatting), with bars grouped by workload and guides at shared group boundaries. All axes are linear and start at zero; ranges differ between panels. Compare bar lengths within a panel; use the numeric labels and tables to compare workloads. Timing bars show medians without whiskers. IQR and SD remain in the tables to show within-run variation; they do not measure between-run reproducibility. Separate speedup tables and plots divide the stdlib median by each backend's median for the same workload, layer, and Python major/minor version. The reference is CPython stdlib JSON; a standalone PyPy report uses PyPy stdlib JSON. Values above 1 mean that the backend was faster in that measurement. Speedups are descriptive ratios without inferred confidence intervals. Only stdlib JSON is measured on PyPy. All runtimes in one workflow invocation share the same runner. Runtime versions and dependencies still differ, and separate invocations can use different hardware. Comparisons do not isolate interpreter performance. Exact patch versions and environments are recorded separately.

docs.title: Update results
docs.text:
The curated baseline consists of one JSON file per Python implementation and version under benchmarks/results/, collected from one workflow invocation. Later workflow runs remain artifacts until explicitly selected as a replacement. Download and extract the benchmark-results artifact from the chosen invocation into benchmark-results/downloaded/. Keep each JSON file under its original name. Curate the files and regenerate the tables:

python scripts/benchmark_report.py benchmark-results/downloaded/*.json \
  --curate benchmarks/results
python scripts/benchmark_report.py benchmarks/results/*.json \
  --update docs/benchmarking.md --plots assets/benchmarking
uv run --no-default-groups --group benchmark-report \
  python scripts/benchmark_plots.py benchmarks/results/*.json \
  --output docs/assets/benchmarking

Curation removes individual timing sample arrays to keep repository files small. It preserves every summary statistic and records the original file’s SHA-256 hash. Workflow artifacts retain the full samples.

Plot generation uses Matplotlib in the separate benchmark-report dependency group; it adds no dependency to timed benchmark runs or ordinary tests. The SVG files contain text labels and can be exported or shared separately. Both plot types are generated from the same committed summaries as the tables.

The generator rejects incomplete or duplicate case matrices. Review the source revision, dependency versions, measurement settings, and variability before committing refreshed data. Artifact retention is finite; the committed curated JSON preserves the measurements used by this page.

docs.title: Baseline results
docs.text:
These measurements come from workflow run 40619767654. Each table records its measured source revision, exact dependency versions, and environment. Some PyPy rounds take milliseconds despite microsecond medians; these outliers are retained and can make SD exceed the mean. These measurements do not identify the cause of the pauses.

Observed repetitions: 8,500–199,721 rounds per case, with 1–100 iterations per round. Warmup and calibration calls are additional.

Within-run SD/mean: 3.9%–5.6e+02% across cases, including outliers. This does not measure between-run variation.

docs.title: Change Log
docs.text:
All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• CI: Use trusted publishing to create PyPI and GitHub releases.
  • Documentation: Quickstart examples are tested to ensure the sample output matches reality.
  • Add support for Python 3.15, PyPy 3.12

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • STYLE_STRING_FORMAT_REGEX, which is no longer used to find { style fields. #75

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Preserve an exception's own notes when encoding exception instances, including exception group summaries. Related to #67.
  • Constrain the documentation dependency to mkdocs<2. #80
  • Replaced MyPy with Pyrefly for type checking

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• exc_info_as_array=True now splits cached exception text into lines when a transported log record has no exc_info tuple. #89
  • BaseJsonFormatter.usesTime() now handles comma-separated and sequence formats, honors custom field parsing, and ignores escaped literal asctime fields. #91
  • % style formats no longer treat the escaped literal %% as the start of a field, so "%%(notafield)s" is correctly read as literal text. #75
  • { style formats now use string.Formatter (as logging.StrFormatStyle.validate does) to find fields, so escaped literal braces ({{/}}) are skipped and a conversion ({message!r}) or format spec ({levelname:>8}) is no longer treated as part of the field name. #75
  • defaults is copied on construction like rename_fields and static_fields, so DictConfigurator ext:// prefixes are converted and mutating the caller's dict cannot change formatter state.
  • A string passed as reserved_attrs raises TypeError instead of being iterated as characters; use a list or tuple of field names.

Thanks @dylanpulver, @Gonghan-Princess, @JackyHsu-X, @00200200, @SAY-5, @AryanRG

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Logging a dict no longer modifies it. exc_info and stack_info were previously added to the caller's dict. #66
  • Move development dependencies from project.optional-dependencies.dev to [dependency-groups].dev (PEP 735). #46

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• $ style formats now support unbraced $name fields, not just ${name}. #18

Thanks @gaoflow, @prateek-dagar, @Sanjays2402

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Add support for Python 3.14, PyPy 3.11

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • Remove support for Python 3.8, 3.9 (includes PyPy versions).

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Support DictConfigurator prefixes for rename_fields and static_fields. #45
    • Allows using values like ext://sys.stderr in fileConfig/dictConfig value fields.
  • Support comma separated lists for Formatter fmt (style=",") e.g. "asctime,message,levelname" #15
    • Note that this style is specific to python-json-logger and thus care should be taken not to pass this format to other logging Formatter implementations.
  • Supports sequences of strings (e.g. lists and tuples) of field names for Formatter fmt. #16

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Rename pythonjsonlogger.core.LogRecord and log_record arguments to avoid confusion / overlapping with logging.LogRecord. #38
    • Affects arguments to pythonjsonlogger.core.BaseJsonFormatter (and any child classes).
      • serialize_log_record
      • add_fields
      • jsonify_log_record
      • process_log_record
    • Note: functions referring to log_record have not had their function name changed.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• Remove support for providing strings instead of objects when instantiating formatters. Instead use the DictConfigurator ext:// prefix format when using fileConfig/dictConfig. #47
    • Affects pythonjsonlogger.json.JsonFormatter: json_default, json_encoder, json_serializer.
    • Affects pythonjsonlogger.orjson.OrjsonFormatter: json_default.
    • Affects pythonjsonlogger.msgspec.MsgspecFormatter: json_default.

Thanks @rubensa

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • exc_info_as_array and stack_info_as_array options are added to pythonjsonlogger.core.BaseJsonFormatter allowing both to be encoded as list of lines instead of a single multi-line string. #35

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Remove msgspec-python313-pre from dev dependencies preventing potential RCE. Details: GHSA-wmxh-pxcx-9w24

Thanks @1hakusai1 and @omnigodz

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Import error on import pythonjsonlogger.jsonlogger #29

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• pythonjsonlogger.[ORJSON,MSGSPEC]_AVAILABLE no longer imports the respective package when determining availability.
  • pythonjsonlogger.[orjson,msgspec] now throws a pythonjsonlogger.exception.MissingPackageError when required libraries are not available. These contain more information about what is missing whilst still being an ImportError.
  • defaults parameter is no longer ignored and now conforms to the standard library. Setting a defaults dictionary will add the specified keys if the those keys do not exist in a record or weren't passed by the extra parameter when logging a message.
  • typing_extensions is only installed on Python version < 3.10.
  • Support Python 3.13
    • msgspec has only been tested against pre-release versions.

Thanks @cjwatson and @bharel
This splits common funcitonality out to allow supporting other JSON encoders. Although this is a large refactor, backwards compatibility has been maintained.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• pythonjsonlogger.core - more details below.
  • pythonjsonlogger.defaults module that provides many functions for handling unsupported types.
  • Orjson encoder support via pythonjsonlogger.orjson.OrjsonFormatter with the following additions:
    • bytes are URL safe base64 encoded.
    • Exceptions are "pretty printed" using the exception name and message e.g. "ValueError: bad value passed"
    • Enum values use their value, Enum classes now return all values as a list.
    • Tracebacks are supported
    • Classes (aka types) are support
    • Will fallback on __str__ if available, else __repr__ if available, else will use __could_not_encode__
  • MsgSpec encoder support via pythonjsonlogger.msgspec.MsgspecFormatter with the following additions:
    • Exceptions are "pretty printed" using the exception name and message e.g. "ValueError: bad value passed"
    • Enum classes now return all values as a list.
    • Tracebacks are supported
    • Classes (aka types) are support
    • Will fallback on __str__ if available, else __repr__ if available, else will use __could_not_encode__
    • Note: msgspec only supprts enum values of type int or str jcrist/msgspec#680

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• pythonjsonlogger.jsonlogger has been moved to pythonjsonlogger.json with core functionality moved to pythonjsonlogger.core.
  • pythonjsonlogger.core.BaseJsonFormatter properly supports all logging.Formatter arguments:
    • fmt is unchanged.
    • datefmt is unchanged.
    • style can now support non-standard arguments by setting validate to False
    • validate allows non-standard style arguments or prevents calling validate on standard style arguments.
    • default is ignored.
  • pythonjsonlogger.json.JsonFormatter default encodings changed:
    • bytes are URL safe base64 encoded.
    • Exception formatting detected using BaseException instead of Exception. Now "pretty prints" the exception using the exception name and message e.g. "ValueError: bad value passed"
    • Dataclasses are now supported
    • Enum values now use their value, Enum classes now return all values as a list.
    • Will fallback on __str__ if available, else __repr__ if available, else will use __could_not_encode__
  • Renaming fields now preserves order (#7) and ignores missing fields (#6).
  • Documentation
    • Generated documentation using mkdocs is stored in docs/
    • Documentation within README.md has been moved to docs/index.md and docs/qucikstart.md.
    • CHANGELOG.md has been moved to docs/change-log.md
    • SECURITY.md has been moved and replaced with a symbolic link to docs/security.md.

docs.title: Generative AI Policy
docs.text:
python-json-logger is a well trusted and popular package. The continued quality, stability, and stewardship of the package is a responsibility that the maintainers take seriously.

Low effort submissions actively work against the maintainers. Every issue and pull request is considered and reviewed by the maintainers, taking a non-trivial amount of time and effort.

The use of AI tools is allowed with the following conditions:

Human Supervision and Responsibility: AI tools must be under supervision of a real human who takes legal and technical responsibility for all contributions made.

This means no fully autonomous systems.

Quality: Ensure that your submission is actually valuable to the project and meets quality expectations. If you cannot explain and defend the changes you submit, do not submit them.

Human Communication: Interactions with the maintainers must be by humans. Don't be a meat-proxy.

AI tools are cheap, if the maintainers want to talk to an AI tool they will use their own.

The only exceptions to this is when a human is interacting with their own AI tools on their own pull requests, or the AI tools of the maintainers. Abuse of this exception will lead to banning.

AI Disclosure: The use of AI tools must be declared.

For issues and pull requests you should append a disclosure similar to the following template:

## AI Disclosure

This <issue,pull-request> was created using: <list of tools and models e.g. 'Hermes, OpenAI models, Calude models, and Deepseek models.>.

Violations: Low quality submissions may be closed without discussion. Repeat offenders will be blocked from the project.

docs.title: Pull Request Process
docs.text:
0. Before you begin

If you're not familiar with contributing to open source software, start by reading this guide.

Be aware that anything you contribute will be licenced under the project's licence. If you are making a change as a part of your job, be aware that your employer might own your work and you'll need their permission in order to licence the code.

docs.title: 1. Find something to work on
docs.text:
Where possible it's best to stick to established issues where discussion has already taken place. Contributions that haven't come from a discussed issue are less likely to be accepted.

The following are things that can be worked on without an existing issue:

  • Updating documentation. This includes fixing in-code documentation / comments, and the overall docs.
  • Small changes that don't change functionality such as refactoring or adding / updating tests.

docs.title: 2. Fork the repository and make your changes
Coding Style
docs.text:
Before writing any code, please familiarize yourself with our Python Style Guide. This document outlines our coding conventions, formatting expectations, and common patterns used in the project. Adhering to this guide is crucial for maintaining code consistency and readability.

While the style guide covers detailed conventions, always try to match the style of existing code in the module you are working on, especially regarding local patterns and structure.

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
All development tooling can be installed (usually into a virtual environment) using uv with the dev dependency group:

uv sync --group dev

Before creating your pull request you'll want to format your code and run the linters and tests:

# Format
black src tests

# Lint
pylint --output-format=colorized src
pyrefly check src tests

# Tests
pytest

The above commands (black, pylint, pyrefly, pytest) should all be run before submitting a pull request.

If making changes to the documentation you can preview the changes locally using mkdocs. Changes to the README.md can be previewed using a tool like grip (installable via pip install grip).

mkdocs serve
# For README preview (after installing grip):
# grip

Note

In general we will always squash merge pull requests so you do not need to worry about a "clean" commit history.

docs.title: 3. Checklist
docs.text:
Before pushing and creating your pull request, you should make sure you've done the following:

  • Updated any relevant tests.
  • Formatted your code and run the linters and tests.
  • Updated the version number in pyproject.toml. In general using a .devN suffix is acceptable. This is not required for changes that do no affect the code such as documentation.
  • Add details of the changes to the change log (docs/change-log.md), creating a new section if needed, and adding youself to the "thanks" section. Changes to documention content should not be added (but changes to documentation tooling should).
  • Add notes for new / changed features in the relevant docstring.

4. Create your pull request

When creating your pull request be aware that the title and description will be used for the final commit so pay attention to them.

Your pull request description should include the following:

  • Why the pull request is being made
  • Summary of changes
  • How the pull request was tested - especially if not covered by unit testing.

Once you've submitted your pull request make sure that all CI jobs are passing. Pull requests with failing jobs will not be reviewed.

docs.title: 5. Code review
docs.text:
Your code will be reviewed by a maintainer.

If you're not familiar with code review start by reading this guide.

Remember you are not your work

You might be asked to explain or justify your choices. This is not a criticism of your value as a person!

Often this is because there are multiple ways to solve the same problem and the reviewer would like to understand more about the way you solved.

docs.title: Adding a new encoder
docs.text:
New encoders may be added depending on their popularity. Only encoders in the top 1000 packages or with monthly downloads exceeding 10M/month will be considered.

You must open an issue before creating a pull request.

For examples of how to support a third-party encoder see orjson.py and msgspec.py.

The following encoders have been considered and rejected:

  • simplejson - as of 2026-03-29 is ranked ~370 with ~55M downloads / month. Due to errors when handling bytes objects and lack of interest from the community (see comment for more details).
  • ultrajson (usjon) - as of 2026-03-29 is ranked ~630 with ~27 downloads / month. Due to errors when handling bytes objects and lack of interest from the community (see comment for more details). Additionally it is in maintenance mode.
  • python-rapidjson - as of 2026-03-22 is ranked ~1800 with ~4.5M downloads / month.
  • pysimdjson - as of 2026-03-22 is ranked ~4200 with >1M downloads / month.
  • yapic.json - as of 2026-03-22 is not in top 15K packages.
  • cysimdjson - as of 2026-03-22 is not in top 15K packages.

docs.title: Versioning and breaking compatibility
docs.text:
This project uses semantic versioning.

In general backwards compatibility is always preferred. This library is widely used and not particularly sophisticated and as such there must be a good reason for breaking changes.

Feature changes MUST be compatible with all security supported versions of Python and SHOULD be compatible with all unsupported versions of Python where recent downloads over the last 90 days exceeds 5% of all downloads.

In general, only the latest major.minor version of Python JSON Logger is supported. Bug fixes and feature backports requiring a version branch may be considered but must be discussed with the maintainers first.

See also Security Policy.

docs.title: Spelling
docs.text:
The original implementation of this project used US spelling so it will continue to use US spelling for all code.

Documentation is more flexible and may use a variety of English spellings.

docs.title: Contacting the Maintainers
docs.text: In general it is preferred to keep communication to GitHub, e.g. through comments on issues and pull requests. If you do need to contact the maintainers privately, please do so using the email addresses in the maintainers section of the pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text: Recipies for common tasks.

docs.title: Include all fields
docs.text:
By default Python JSON Logger will not include fields defined in the standard library unless they are included in the format. Manually including all these fields is tedious and Python version specific. Instead of adding them as explicit fields, we can add them implicitly be ensuring they are not in the reserver_attrs argument of the formatter.

all_fields_formatter = JsonFormatter(reserved_attrs=[])

docs.title: Custom Styles
docs.text:
It is possible to support custom styles by setting validate=False and overriding the parse method.

For example:

class CommaSupport(JsonFormatter):
    def parse(self) -> list[str]:
        if isinstance(self._style, str) and self._style == ",":
            return self._fmt.split(",")
        return super().parse()

formatter = CommaSupport("message,asctime", style=",", validate=False)

docs.title: Modifying the logged data
docs.text:
You can modify the dict of data that will be logged by overriding the process_log_record method to modify fields before they are serialized to JSON.

class SillyFormatter(JsonFormatter):
    def process_log_record(self, log_data):
        new_record = {k[::-1]: v for k, v in log_data.items()}
        return new_record

docs.title: Logging exceptions, exception groups, and exception notes
docs.text:
Use exc_info=True inside an exception handler to include a traceback in a JSON log record. This preserves exception notes, including notes on exception groups and their members.

The following example requires Python 3.11 or later for add_note() and ExceptionGroup. It uses exc_info_as_array=True to represent the traceback as an array of lines. With the default False, the same information is included in a single string containing newline characters.

import logging
from pythonjsonlogger.json import JsonFormatter

logger = logging.getLogger("exception_example")
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
logger.propagate = False
handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter(exc_info_as_array=True))
logger.addHandler(handler)

error = ValueError("invalid value")
error.add_note("Check the input value.")

other_error = RuntimeError("operation failed")
other_error.add_note("Retry the operation.")

group = ExceptionGroup("multiple errors", [error, other_error])
group.add_note("Errors occurred during processing.")

try:
    raise error
except ValueError:
    logger.info("Exception with traceback", exc_info=True)

try:
    raise group
except ExceptionGroup:
    logger.info("Exception group with traceback", exc_info=True)

logger.info({"message": "Exception as a value", "error": error})
logger.info({"message": "Exception group as a value", "error": group})

The first call with exc_info=True includes the exception's traceback and note:

{
  "message": "Exception with traceback",
  "exc_info": [
    "Traceback (most recent call last):",
    "  File \"<string>\", line 21, in <module>",
    "    raise error",
    "ValueError: invalid value",
    "Check the input value."
  ]
}

The second includes the group's traceback, its own note, and both members with their notes:

{
  "message": "Exception group with traceback",
  "exc_info": [
    "  + Exception Group Traceback (most recent call last):",
    "  |   File \"<string>\", line 26, in <module>",
    "  |     raise group",
    "  | ExceptionGroup: multiple errors (2 sub-exceptions)",
    "  | Errors occurred during processing.",
    "  +-+---------------- 1 ----------------",
    "    | Traceback (most recent call last):",
    "    |   File \"<string>\", line 21, in <module>",
    "    |     raise error",
    "    | ValueError: invalid value",
    "    | Check the input value.",
    "    +---------------- 2 ----------------",
    "    | RuntimeError: operation failed",
    "    | Retry the operation.",
    "    +------------------------------------"
  ]
}

Traceback paths, line numbers, source excerpts, and presentation can vary with the script location and Python version. These examples show output from running the code with python -c.

Passing an exception as a dictionary value uses the encoder's default exception serialization instead of traceback formatting. It includes the exception's name, message, and own notes, without a traceback:

{
  "message": "Exception as a value",
  "error": "ValueError: invalid value\nCheck the input value."
}

For an exception group, this produces the group summary and its own notes. It does not recursively include members or their notes:

{
  "message": "Exception group as a value",
  "error": "ExceptionGroup: multiple errors (2 sub-exceptions)\nErrors occurred during processing."
}

docs.title: Request / Trace IDs
docs.text:
There are many ways to add consistent request IDs to your logging. The exact method will depend on your needs and application.

## Common Setup
## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
import logging
import uuid
from pythonjsonlogger.json import JsonFormatter

logger = logging.getLogger("test")
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)
handler = logging.StreamHandler()
logger.addHandler(handler)

One method would be to inject the request ID into each log call using the extra argument. 

## Solution 1
## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
formatter = JsonFormatter()
handler.setFormatter(formatter)

def main_1():
    print("========== MAIN 1 ==========")
    for i in range(3):
        request_id = uuid.uuid4()
        logger.info("loop start", extra={"request_id": request_id})
        logger.info(f"loop {i}", extra={"request_id": request_id})
        logger.info("loop end", extra={"request_id": request_id})
    return

main_1()

Another method would be to use a filter to modify the LogRecord attributes. This would also allow us to use it in any other standard logging machinery. For this example I've manually set a REQUEST_ID global and some helper functions, but you might already have stuff available to you; for example, if you're using a web-framework with baked in request IDs.

This is based on the logging cookbook filter recipie.

## Solution 2
## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
REQUEST_ID: str | None = None

def get_request_id() -> str:
    return REQUEST_ID

def generate_request_id():
    global REQUEST_ID
    REQUEST_ID = str(uuid.uuid4())

class RequestIdFilter(logging.Filter):
    def filter(self, record):
        record.request_id = get_request_id() # Add request_id to the LogRecord
        return True

request_id_filter = RequestIdFilter()
logger.addFilter(request_id_filter)

def main_2():
    print("========== MAIN 2 ==========")
    for i in range(3):
        generate_request_id()
        logger.info("loop start")
        logger.info(f"loop {i}")
        logger.info("loop end")
    return

main_2()

logger.removeFilter(request_id_filter)

Another method would be to create a custom formatter class and override the process_log_record method. This allows us to inject fields into the record before we log it without modifying the original LogRecord.

## Solution 3
## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reuse REQUEST_ID stuff from solution 2
class MyFormatter(JsonFormatter):
    def process_log_record(self, log_data):
        log_data["request_id"] = get_request_id()
        return log_data

handler.setFormatter(MyFormatter())

def main_3():
    print("========== MAIN 3 ==========")
    for i in range(3):
        generate_request_id()
        logger.info("loop start")
        logger.info(f"loop {i}")
        logger.info("loop end")
    return

main_3()

docs.title: Using fileConfig
docs.text:
To use the module with a yaml config file using the fileConfig function, use the class pythonjsonlogger.json.JsonFormatter. Here is a sample config file:

example_config.yaml
version: 1
disable_existing_loggers: False
formatters:
  default:
    "()": pythonjsonlogger.json.JsonFormatter
    format: "%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(module)s %(funcName)s %(lineno)s %(message)s"
    json_default: ext://logging_config.my_json_default
    rename_fields:
      "asctime": "timestamp"
      "levelname": "status"
    static_fields:
      "service": ext://logging_config.PROJECT_NAME
      "env": ext://logging_config.ENVIRONMENT
      "version": ext://logging_config.PROJECT_VERSION
      "app_log": "true"
handlers:
  default:
    formatter: default
    class: logging.StreamHandler
    stream: ext://sys.stderr
  access:
    formatter: default
    class: logging.StreamHandler
    stream: ext://sys.stdout
loggers:
  uvicorn.error:
    level: INFO
    handlers:
      - default
    propagate: no
  uvicorn.access:
    level: INFO
    handlers:
      - access
    propagate: no

You'll notice that we are using ext://... for json_default andstatic_fields. This will load data from other modules such as the one below.

logging_config.py
import importlib.metadata
import os


class Dummy:
    pass


def my_json_default(obj: Any) -> Any:
    if isinstance(obj, Dummy):
        return "DUMMY"
    return obj


def get_version_metadata():
    # https://stackoverflow.com/a/78082532
    version = importlib.metadata.version(PROJECT_NAME)
    return version


PROJECT_NAME = 'test-api'
PROJECT_VERSION = get_version_metadata()
ENVIRONMENT = os.environ.get('ENVIRONMENT', 'dev')

docs.title: Logging Expensive to Compute Data
docs.text:
By the nature of Python's logging library, the JSON formatters will only ever run in handlers which are enabled for the given log level. This saves the performance hit of constructing JSON that is never used - but what about the data we pass into the logger? There are two options available to us: using if statements to avoid the call altogether, or using lazy string evaluation libraries.

Note

The below strategies will work for data passed in the msg and extra arguments.

To avoid the logging calls we use logger.isEnabledFor to ensure that we only start constructing our log messages if the logger is enabled:

import logging
import time

from pythonjsonlogger.json import JsonFormatter

def expensive_to_compute():
    time.sleep(5)
    return "world"

## Setup
## -------------------------------------
logger = logging.getLogger()
handler = logging.StreamHandler()
formatter = JsonFormatter()
handler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.addHandler(handler)
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

## Log Using isEnabledFor
## -------------------------------------
start = time.time()
if logger.isEnabledFor(logging.INFO):
    logger.info(
        {
            "data": "hello {}".format(expensive_to_compute())
        }
    )
print(f"Logging INFO using isEnabledFor took: {int(time.time() - start)}s")

start = time.time()
if logger.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG):
    logger.debug(
        {
            "data": "hello {}".format(expensive_to_compute())
        }
    )
print(f"Logging DEBUG using isEnabledFor took: {int(time.time() - start)}s")

For lazy string evaluation we can take advantage of the fact that the default JSON encoders included in this package will call str on unkown objects. We can use this to build our own lazy string evaluators, or we can use an existing external package. Pre-existing solutions include: lazy-string's LazyString or stringlike's CachedLazyString.

## Log Using lazy-string
## -------------------------------------
from lazy_string import LazyString as L

start = time.time()
logger.info(
    {
        "data": L("hello {}".format, L(expensive_to_compute))
    }
)
print(f"Logging INFO using LazyString took: {int(time.time() - start)}s")

start = time.time()
logger.debug(
    {
        "data": L("hello {}".format, L(expensive_to_compute))
    }
)
print(f"Logging DEBUG using LazyString took: {int(time.time() - start)}s")

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Note

All versions of this fork use version >=3.0.0.

To use pre-fork versions use python-json-logger<3.

docs.title: Install via pip
docs.text: pip install python-json-logger

docs.title: Install from GitHub
docs.text:
To install from releases (including development releases), you can use the URL to the specific wheel.

# e.g. 3.0.0 wheel
pip install 'python-json-logger@https://github.com/nhairs/python-json-logger/releases/download/v3.0.0/python_json_logger-3.0.0-py3-none-any.whl'

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: Python JSON Logger provides logging.Formatter classes that encode the logged message into JSON. Although a variety of JSON encoders are supported, the following examples will use the JsonFormatter which uses the the json module from the standard library.

docs.title: Integrating with Python's logging framework
docs.text:
To produce JSON output, attach the formatter to a logging handler:

import logging
from pythonjsonlogger.json import JsonFormatter

logger = logging.getLogger()
logger.setLevel(logging.INFO)

logHandler = logging.StreamHandler()
formatter = JsonFormatter()
logHandler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.addHandler(logHandler)

docs.title: Required Fields
docs.text:
You can control the logged fields by setting the fmt argument when creating the formatter. A variety of different formats are supported including:

  • Standard library formats: where style is one of %, $, or {. This allows using Python JSON Logger Formatters with your existing config.
  • Comma format: where style is , which simplifies the writing of formats where you can't use more complex formats.
  • A sequence of string: e.g. lists or tuples.

All LogRecord attributes can be output using their name.

# Standard library format
formatter = JsonFormatter("{message}{asctime}{exc_info}", style="{")

# Comma format
formatter = JsonFormatter("message,asctime,exc_info", style=",")

# Sequence of strings format
formatter = JsonFormatter(["message", "asctime", "exc_info"])

docs.title: Message Fields
docs.text:
Instead of logging a string message you can log using a dict.

logger.info({
    "my_data": 1,
    "message": "if you don't include this it will be an empty string",
    "other_stuff": False,
})

Warning

Be aware that if you log using a dict, other formatters may not be able to handle it.

Note

Your dict is not modified when the formatter adds fields such as exc_info.

You can also add additional message fields using the extra argument.

logger.info(
    "this logs the same additional fields as above",
    extra={
        "my_data": 1,
        "other_stuff": False,
    },
)

Finally, any non-standard attributes added to a LogRecord will also be included in the logged data. See Cookbook: Request / Trace IDs for an example.

For exceptions passed as dictionary values, see Logging exceptions, exception groups, and exception notes for how their output differs from logging with exc_info=True.

docs.title: Default Fields
docs.text:
Default fields that are added to every log record prior to any other field can be set using the defaults argument.

formatter = JsonFormatter(
    defaults={"environment": "dev"}
)
logHandler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.info("this message will have environment=dev by default")
logger.info("this overwrites the environment field", extra={"environment": "prod"})

Output:

{"environment": "dev", "message": "this message will have environment=dev by default"}
{"environment": "prod", "message": "this overwrites the environment field"}

docs.title: Static Fields
docs.text:
Static fields that are added to every log record can be set using the static_fields argument.

formatter = JsonFormatter(
    static_fields={"service": "billing"}
)
logHandler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.info("processing a request")

Output:

{"message": "processing a request", "service": "billing"}

Despite the name, static fields can be overridden by message fields and extra fields, as described below.

docs.title: Field Precedence
docs.text:
These field sources are added in the following order. A later source replaces an earlier value for the same output key:

  1. defaults
  2. Fields selected by fmt
  3. static_fields
  4. Fields from a dictionary message
  5. Non-reserved LogRecord attributes, including those supplied through extra

Fields selected by fmt are handled in step 2 and are not merged again in step 5. This is why static_fields can override a field selected by fmt, even when that field was supplied through extra. All five sources are subject to rename_fields.

The following example shows a static value overriding both a default and the record's levelname, while dictionary messages and extra can override the static environment:

formatter = JsonFormatter(
    ["message", "levelname"],
    defaults={"environment": "dev", "levelname": "DEFAULT"},
    static_fields={"environment": "test", "levelname": "STATIC"},
)
logHandler.setFormatter(formatter)
logger.info("static fields win over defaults and fmt")
logger.info({"message": "dictionary message wins", "environment": "staging"})
logger.info(
    {"message": "extra wins", "environment": "staging"},
    extra={"environment": "prod"},
)

Output:

{"environment": "test", "levelname": "STATIC", "message": "static fields win over defaults and fmt"}
{"environment": "staging", "levelname": "STATIC", "message": "dictionary message wins"}
{"environment": "prod", "levelname": "STATIC", "message": "extra wins"}

docs.title: Excluding fields
docs.text:
You can prevent fields being added to the output data by adding them to reserved_attrs. By default all LogRecord attributes are excluded.

from pythonjsonlogger.core import RESERVED_ATTRS

formatter = JsonFormatter(
    reserved_attrs=RESERVED_ATTRS+["request_id", "my_other_field"]
)

docs.title: Renaming fields
docs.text:
You can rename fields using the rename_fields argument.

formatter = JsonFormatter(
    "{message}{levelname}",
    style="{",
    rename_fields={"levelname": "LEVEL"},
)

docs.title: Custom object serialization
docs.text:
Most formatters support json_default which is used to control how objects are serialized.

def my_default(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, MyClass):
        return {"special": obj.special}

formatter = JsonFormatter(json_default=my_default)

Note

When providing your own json_default, you likely want to call the original json_default for your encoder. Python JSON Logger provides custom default serializers for each encoder that tries very hard to ensure sane output is always logged.

docs.title: Alternate JSON Encoders
docs.text:
The following JSON encoders are also supported:

  • orjson - pythonjsonlogger.orjson.OrjsonFormatter
  • msgspec - pythonjsonlogger.msgspec.MsgspecFormatter

docs.title: Release checklist
docs.text: The release.yml workflow checks eligibility, runs CI, builds distributions, and stages a GitHub draft. After pypi approval, it uploads to PyPI and verifies both files before publishing GitHub.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• [ ] Set project.version in pyproject.toml.
  • [ ] Update the base-version section in docs/changelog.md. Set YYYY-MM-DD for RCs and stable releases; only development releases may use UNRELEASED. Post releases must match the date at the base release tag.
  • [ ] Merge the release commit into main.
  • [ ] Review and push the tag. Use vN.N.N with optional .devN, .rcN, or .postN, without leading zeros.

For example, v4.3.0.rc1 matches project version 4.3.0rc1 and the 4.3.0 changelog section. Alpha, beta, undotted suffixes, and combined suffixes are rejected. Exact validation blocks invalid releases; it does not prevent tag creation.

git tag v4.3.0.rc1
git push origin v4.3.0.rc1

Before lint or tests, eligibility rejects any PyPI record for the target version, including partial or yanked releases. Only HTTP 404 means absent; service and network errors stop the run. A public GitHub release also blocks a new attempt and requires owner cleanup. Existing drafts are allowed.

docs.title: Approve
docs.text:
• [ ] Check lint and the Linux, macOS, and Windows test results.
  • [ ] Review the GitHub draft: title, full changelog, and prerelease flag.
  • [ ] Check the wheel, sdist, SHA256SUMS.json, and release.json assets.
  • [ ] Approve the pypi deployment.
  • [ ] Confirm PyPI has both files and GitHub is published.

Every build attempt creates fresh distributions. Staging replaces all assets on a same-commit draft, or deletes and recreates a draft for a different commit. Cleanup happens after checks and build succeed. Public releases are never replaced.

After approval, publication readiness repeats the same version-eligibility policy: the live tag must still match, GitHub must remain unpublished, and PyPI must have no version record. It also verifies the built bundle's identity and checksums and compares every draft asset against that bundle. The early check allows no draft or an obsolete draft; readiness requires the exact staged build. PyPI absence is checked last, after the asset comparison.

The approved job uses OIDC to upload the complete distribution set. It checks out only scripts/release.py at the run's commit without persisting checkout credentials. The shared Python checks run with isolation enabled and use only the standard library. A separate finalization job verifies both PyPI filenames and hashes before publishing the original draft. Keep the Trusted Publisher repository, workflow filename release.yml, and pypi environment unchanged.

docs.title: Recover before any PyPI upload
docs.text:
• [ ] Check PyPI to confirm no file for the version was accepted.
  • [ ] Cancel an obsolete run waiting for approval before starting its replacement.
  • [ ] Fix and merge the workflow or source change, then retarget the unpublished tag under the repository's protection rules, or rerun the original run for a transient failure with unchanged source.
  • [ ] Review the fresh build and draft, then approve the new deployment.

Runs are serialized per tag without automatic cancellation; different tags run independently. The owner cancels stale waiting runs manually. If approved instead, a stale run fails its recheck when the tag moved or another run published PyPI. Avoid moving tags during an active upload. Rechecks cannot lock a tag against an owner changing it after the check.

docs.title: Recover after a PyPI upload
docs.text:
Any accepted file freezes the version's source and distribution bytes. Normal attempts stop rather than rebuild, select missing files, or use skip-existing. Deleting a PyPI version does not guarantee its filenames can be uploaded again.

If the PyPI step succeeded but GitHub finalization failed:

  1. Select Re-run failed jobs on the original run. This reruns finalization with the original build artifact ID without uploading to PyPI again.
  2. Confirm finalization verifies the complete PyPI hashes and original draft assets.
  3. Confirm the GitHub release is published.

Do not select Re-run all jobs after publication: eligibility rejects the existing version. If PyPI accepted files but the upload step failed, or an upload was partial, stop automatic recovery. Recover the original distributions and manifest from the draft or retained bundle for an owner-reviewed manual recovery. This workflow does not automate partial uploads. If the original bytes cannot be recovered, prepare a new version.

docs.title: Retained artifacts
docs.text:
Artifact Contents release-bundle-N Original wheel and sdist, SHA256SUMS.json, full notes, and release.json with tag, version, commit, build run, and attempt. finalization-evidence-N Original bundle artifact ID and GitHub finalization outcome. publication-evidence-N Available .publish.attestation files, manifest, release metadata, bundle artifact ID, publication attempt, and step outcomes.

N is the job's workflow attempt. Artifacts are retained for 90 days and scoped to the workflow run. Downstream jobs use the exact build artifact ID, including when a failed job reruns with a newer attempt number. The old pypi-upload-N subset artifact is no longer needed because normal publication uploads both files.

Evidence retention runs even after failure. If signing never started, the evidence records that no attestations are available. Distributions remain in the referenced bundle and GitHub draft. No credentials, OIDC tokens, or private keys are archived.

Saved attestations bind the CI identity to exact distribution hashes; they are not upload credentials. PyPI requires Trusted Publishing authentication to accept these attestations. Ordinary local API-token uploads cannot replay that identity. The publishing action generates fresh attestations and rejects pre-existing attestation files when generation is enabled. Preserve evidence for investigation and future recovery rather than assuming it can be submitted by a local upload.

docs.title: Python Style Guide
docs.text: This document outlines the coding style, conventions, and common patterns for the python-json-logger project. Adhering to this guide will help maintain code consistency, readability, and quality.

docs.title: General Principles
docs.text:
• Readability Counts: Write code that is easy for others (and your future self) to understand. This aligns with PEP 20 (The Zen of Python).
  • Consistency: Strive for consistency in naming, formatting, and structure throughout the codebase.
  • Simplicity: Prefer simple, straightforward solutions over overly complex ones.
  • PEP 8: Follow PEP 8 (Style Guide for Python Code) for all Python code. The automated tools mentioned below will enforce many of these rules. This guide highlights project-specific conventions or particularly important PEP 8 aspects.

docs.title: Formatting and Linting
docs.text:
We use automated tools to enforce a consistent code style and catch potential errors. These include:

  • Black: For opinionated code formatting.
  • Pylint: For static code analysis and error detection.
  • Pyrefly: For static type checking.

Ensure these tools are run before committing code. Configuration for these tools can be found in pyproject.toml, pylintrc, and pyrefly.toml respectively. This guide primarily focuses on conventions not automatically verifiable by these tools.

docs.title: Imports
docs.text:
Imports should be structured into the following groups, separated by a blank line, and generally alphabetized within each group:

  1. Future Imports: e.g., from __future__ import annotations
  2. Standard Library Imports: e.g., import sys, from datetime import datetime
  3. Installed (Third-Party) Library Imports: e.g., import pytest
  4. Application (Local) Imports: e.g., from .core import BaseJsonFormatter (This project-specific pattern is crucial for internal organization).

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
While PEP 8 covers most naming, we emphasize:

  • Modules: lowercase_with_underscores.py
  • Packages: lowercase
  • Classes & Type Aliases: CapWords (e.g., BaseJsonFormatter, OptionalCallableOrStr). This is standard, but explicitly stated for clarity.
  • Constants: UPPERCASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES (e.g., RESERVED_ATTRS). This is a project convention for module-level constants.

(Functions, methods, and variables follow standard PEP 8 lowercase_with_underscores).

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Use comments to explain non-obvious code, complex logic, or important design decisions. Avoid comments that merely restate what the code does.
  • For internal code organization within files, especially in longer modules or classes, use comments like ## Section Title ## or ### Subsection Title ### to delineate logical blocks of code (e.g., ## Parent Methods ## as seen in src/pythonjsonlogger/core.py). This is distinct from Markdown headings used in this document.

docs.title: Docstrings
docs.text:
• All public modules, classes, functions, and methods must have docstrings.
  • We use mkdocstrings for generating API documentation, which defaults to the Google Python Style Guide for docstrings. Please adhere to this style. You can find the guide here.
  • Docstrings should clearly explain the purpose, arguments, return values, and any exceptions raised.
  • Project Convention: Use the following markers to indicate changes over time: * *New in version_number*: For features added in a specific version. * *Changed in version_number*: For changes made in a specific version. * *Deprecated in version_number*: For features deprecated in a specific version.

    Example: 

    def my_function(param1: str, param2: int) -> bool:
    """Does something interesting.

    Args:
        param1: The first parameter, a string.
        param2: The second parameter, an integer.

    Returns:
        True if successful, False otherwise.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If param2 is negative.

    *New in 3.1*
    """
    # ... function logic ...
    return True # See 'Return Statements'

docs.title: Type Hinting
docs.text:
• All new code must include type hints for function arguments, return types, and variables where appropriate, as per PEP 484.
  • Use standard types from the typing module.
  • Project Convention: For Python versions older than 3.10, use typing_extensions.TypeAlias for creating type aliases. For Python 3.10+, use typing.TypeAlias (e.g., OptionalCallableOrStr: TypeAlias = ...).

docs.title: Return Statements
docs.text:
• Project Convention: All functions and methods must have an explicit return statement.
  • If a function does not logically return a value, it should end with return None or simply return. This makes the intent clear and consistent across the codebase.

    Example: 

    def process_data(data: dict) -> None:
    """Processes the given data."""
    # ... processing logic ...
    print(data)
    return # or return None

docs.title: Class Structure
docs.text:
• Group methods logically within a class (e.g., initialization, public, protected/private, special methods).
  • The use of internal code comments like ## Parent Methods ## (as seen in src/pythonjsonlogger/core.py) is encouraged for readability in complex classes.

docs.title: Project-Specific Code Patterns and Idioms
docs.text:
Familiarize yourself with these patterns commonly used in this project:

  • Version-Specific Logic: Using sys.version_info for compatibility: 
    if sys.version_info >= (3, 10):
    # Python 3.10+ specific code
else:
    # Code for older versions
  • Type Aliases for Clarity: As mentioned in Type Hinting, using TypeAlias for complex type combinations improves readability.
  • Custom Exceptions: Defining custom exception classes for application-specific error conditions (e.g., MissingPackageError in src/pythonjsonlogger/exception.py).
  • Helper/Utility Functions: Encapsulating reusable logic in utility modules (e.g., functions in src/pythonjsonlogger/utils.py).
  • Conditional Imports for Optional Dependencies: The pattern in src/pythonjsonlogger/__init__.py for checking optional dependencies like orjson and msgspec using package_is_available from utils.py.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
This project uses pytest for testing. Adherence to good testing practices is crucial.

  • Test Location: Tests are located in the tests/ directory.
  • Test Naming: Test files test_*.py; test functions test_*.
  • Fixtures: Utilize pytest fixtures (@pytest.fixture) for setup. * Project Pattern: The LoggingEnvironment dataclass and env fixture in tests/test_formatters.py is a key pattern for testing logger behavior. Adapt this for similar scenarios.
  • Parametrization: Use @pytest.mark.parametrize extensively to cover multiple scenarios efficiently.
  • Clarity and Focus: Each test should be focused and its name descriptive.
  • Assertions: Use clear, specific pytest assertions.

By following these guidelines, we can ensure that python-json-logger remains a high-quality, maintainable, and developer-friendly library.

docs.title: Logging Time
docs.text:
Python JSON Logger supports two ways to include the time a log record was created:

Option How to enable it Default representation timestamp Pass timestamp=True to the formatter A UTC datetime serialized by the JSON encoder asctime Include %(asctime)s in the format A local-time string formatted by Python's logging.Formatter

Neither is included by default. Both use the record's creation time, not the time at which a handler formats it.

docs.title: UTC timestamps
docs.text:
Use timestamp=True for a UTC timestamp without customizing the standard library's time formatter. With pythonjsonlogger.json.JsonFormatter and its default encoder, the result is an ISO 8601 string, not a Unix epoch number. Fractional seconds are included when nonzero.

The examples below use a record with a fixed creation time so that the output is reproducible. In an application, attach the formatter to a handler as shown in the quick start.

import logging

from pythonjsonlogger.json import JsonFormatter

record = logging.makeLogRecord(
    {"msg": "Hello", "args": (), "created": 1500000000.125, "msecs": 125.0}
)
formatter = JsonFormatter(timestamp=True)
print(formatter.format(record))

{"message": "Hello", "timestamp": "2017-07-14T02:40:00.125000+00:00"}

Pass a nonempty string to choose a different output field name:

formatter = JsonFormatter(timestamp="time")
print(formatter.format(record))

{"message": "Hello", "time": "2017-07-14T02:40:00.125000+00:00"}

The field does not need to appear in fmt. Conversely, including %(timestamp)s in fmt does not enable timestamp generation. Without timestamp=True or a value supplied on the record, it produces null:

formatter = JsonFormatter("%(message)s %(timestamp)s")
print(formatter.format(record))

{"message": "Hello", "timestamp": null}

The formatter adds an aware UTC datetime to the data before JSON serialization. Other encoders or a custom encoder may represent that datetime differently. Neither datefmt nor converter changes this value.

docs.title: Standard-library time formatting with asctime
docs.text:
Use asctime when you need the standard library's datefmt or converter behavior. By default, logging.Formatter uses local time and a format such as 2017-07-14 02:40:00,125.

Set converter to time.gmtime for UTC. The following example reuses the record above and sets UTC explicitly so that its output does not depend on the machine's local time zone:

import time

formatter = JsonFormatter("%(message)s %(asctime)s", datefmt="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
formatter.converter = time.gmtime
print(formatter.format(record))

{"message": "Hello", "asctime": "2017-07-14T02:40:00Z"}

datefmt uses time.strftime, not datetime.strftime. In particular, %f is not supported for formatting fractional seconds here. A supplied datefmt replaces the default time format, including its automatic millisecond suffix. For further customization, override logging.Formatter.formatTime.

Renaming asctime with rename_fields={"asctime": "timestamp"} only changes its field name; it does not turn the formatted string into a UTC datetime. You can enable both asctime and timestamp, but give them distinct output names: a generated timestamp overwrites an earlier value using the same output key, including a renamed asctime field.

docs.title: Configure timestamps with dictConfig
docs.text:
No custom formatter subclass is needed to enable timestamp through logging.config.dictConfig. Pass it as a formatter option alongside format:

import logging.config

logging.config.dictConfig(
    {
        "version": 1,
        "disable_existing_loggers": False,
        "formatters": {
            "json": {
                "()": "pythonjsonlogger.json.JsonFormatter",
                "format": "%(levelname)s %(message)s",
                "timestamp": True,
            }
        },
        "handlers": {
            "console": {
                "class": "logging.StreamHandler",
                "formatter": "json",
            }
        },
        "loggers": {
            "example": {"handlers": ["console"], "level": "INFO", "propagate": False}
        },
    }
)
logging.getLogger("example").info("Hello")

This emits levelname, message, and timestamp; the timestamp reflects the actual log record's creation time. Use "timestamp": "time" instead to select a different key. In a YAML configuration loaded for dictConfig, use timestamp: true (a boolean), not timestamp: "true" (which selects the field name "true").
